prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how productivity differences shape who exports and invests abroad and how trade reallocates resources across firms

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B014 with Melitz and Helpman. I re-tested it against the round-1 exchange and the chair's questions rather than relying on my opening rank. The heterogeneous-firm framework is a single, bounded discovery. Productivity-sorted firms self-select into exporting and foreign investment, and trade then reallocates resources toward more productive firms. That created a new channel for the gains from trade, and it came with testable predictions that were confirmed in firm-level microdata in many countries over twenty years. It is a case of theory built to be tested, which is the kind of contribution I value from my own work on contracting theory tested against real contracts. Maturity is not in question. The attribution problem is of a different kind from the one in B009. It concerns who else deserves credit, not which discovery is being credited. Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) is its first major extension, so the two-name set covers the core model and its main extension. I have tightened the citation to selection and reallocation, so it does not claim a large aggregate welfare effect or the empirical exporter-premia and quantitative-trade lines. In my own reading, B009 is a very strong rival on merit. What separates the two for me is how cleanly each can be written as one citation, not the quality of the science.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is priority. Bernard and Jensen (exporter premia), Eaton and Kortum (quantitative Ricardian trade) and Hopenhayn (firm dynamics) have serious claims to adjacent parts of the firm-level revolution, and the two-name set credits none of them. A narrow citation limits the damage but does not remove it. I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the earlier new trade theory. Helpman's separate B049 candidacy complicates how his credit is framed. The Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare results show that the aggregate welfare gain from selection depends on functional-form assumptions and may be smaller than first claimed. On B009, the round-1 exchange raised a point I take seriously: its identification in the trade-shock strand is sharper than the evidence behind some B014 welfare claims, and B009 has the broadest support. That is a real argument for B009 and I do not dismiss it. I also have no way to show that a committee majority would find B014's priority problem easier to live with than B009's Dorn-or-Katz and bundling problem.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B014 sixth because Krugman's 2008 prize covers part of the antecedent trade theory, because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited, and because the size of the welfare gains from selection is contested. She asked Boppart, Friberg and me how we weigh these against the framework's reach.
responses.response: I weigh them as qualifications on the citation, and the priority point most heavily. Krugman's prize recognised scale economies, product differentiation and trade patterns with representative firms. Melitz moved the unit of analysis to productivity-sorted firms and put selection and reallocation at the centre, which is a different object. On welfare, the Arkolakis et al. result narrows how much of the headline gain comes from selection under particular assumptions. It also shows the framework made the welfare calculation tractable, and the margins of adjustment still matter for reallocation and distribution. That is why my citation says selection and reallocation and makes no claim about aggregate gains. Priority is the part that does not fully resolve. A citation limited to selection into exporting and FDI avoids claiming the exporter-premia facts or the Ricardian quantitative line, but it cannot give Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum the credit they may deserve. Two things would move me to B009. One is a committee finding that those claims are decisive. The other is a single concrete B009 citation that withstands the Dorn-or-Katz and bundling objections.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B009 first and B014 fourth. He calls Melitz-Helpman mature and cleanly paired, but he is held back by Krugman's 2008 prize and by the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Eaton and Kortum. He also argues that B009's designs are sharper and that Katz is needed to cover technology, trade and wage inequality together.
responses.response: We agree on the facts and differ mainly on which attribution risk to accept. Your Katz argument is also the reason B009 is hard to write as one citation. A prize that needs Katz to cover technology, trade and wage inequality credits a broad account assembled from strands with partly different people behind them. The narrow variant credits Autor, Dorn and Hanson but drops the framework you value. B014 has the opposite problem. Its discovery is fixed and the question is who else is owed credit. I accept your point that identification in the trade-shock designs is more transparent than the structural welfare claims in B014. That is a real advantage for B009 and it keeps B009 as my first alternative. It does not change my preference, because for me the single, bounded discovery matters more than the transparency of one strand. I would not call the difference large.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. After reading Friberg he is more positive on B014. He says Krugman's 2008 prize concerned trade patterns and geography and not firm selection, and he names the priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum and Helpman's split B049 candidacy as the unresolved issues.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of Krugman 2008 and with your two unresolved issues. On B049 I would handle the split by wording. The Helpman rationale here is the heterogeneous-firm and exports-versus-FDI work with Melitz and Yeaple, which stands apart from the political economy of trade policy. I do not want one prize to carry both. Your Autor-Dorn-Hanson variant is the most defensible attribution of the trade-shock design, and you say plainly that it narrows the prize to one programme. I think the exchange has made that trade-off clear. A broader B009 needs Katz, a narrower one needs Dorn, and the committee has to choose the discovery before it can choose the names. Where I differ is that the B014 discovery needs no such choice. I treat that as evidence about how well the prize can be bounded and not as evidence of scientific merit.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B009 first and B014 close behind. He says B014 has more diffuse priority issues and that welfare-gain magnitudes depend on modelling assumptions. He leans toward treating the technology and trade strands of B009 as one explanation of changing labour demand.
responses.response: I accept that B014's priority issues are real, and that welfare magnitudes are model-dependent. I would call the priority issues bounded and not diffuse. They concern adjacent contributions whose authors the committee could acknowledge in the scientific background, while the identity of the core model and its first extension is not disputed. Your lean toward one explanation for B009 is the strongest version of that case, and if the committee adopts it I would take Autor, Hanson and Katz as the right trio. That is the configuration I proposed in my opening, and I would rank it just behind B014. My residual doubt is that Autor is the only person spanning both strands, and the shift-share persistence debate sits on the strand with the most recent evidence. I would not want the citation to rest on the strand that is least settled.

uncertainties: Whether the priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum and Hopenhayn are strong enough that a Melitz-Helpman citation overstates the novelty of the heterogeneous-firm framework, and whether narrow wording is an adequate answer.
How much of the welfare-gain claim survives the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare critique, and whether it affects the prize-level importance of the framework or only the size of the claimed effect.
Whether Krugman's 2008 prize and Helpman's separate B049 candidacy make B014 look partly rewarded, even though I judge the discoveries distinct.

For B009, whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery or two. If the committee defines them as one, I would support Autor, Hanson and Katz. If it defines the discovery as the China shock, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson. I cannot judge from the evidence which framing a majority will adopt.
How the committee reads the overlap of B009 with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. Members describe those prizes differently, and I am not certain the overlap is only thematic.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names on B014 (Melitz, Helpman), B009 or B040. The profile records no co-authorship or institutional tie to any of them. Documented connections are my adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth, my principal co-authorship with Steven Kaplan and others in corporate finance, my long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell and other colleagues, and my role as Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. None of these links to a candidate on my preferred or alternative parts. As in round 1, I rely on the supplied profile, claim no independent verification, and disclose without adjudicating.
